domain: Transportation Systems / Institutional Coordination / Path Dependence
topic_summary: Analysis of the convention governing which side of the road vehicles travel on, focusing on right-hand driving as the dominant global standard. The topic examines how an arbitrary coordination choice becomes locked in through network effects, infrastructure investment, and cross-border standardization pressures.

key_entities: Right-hand traffic convention (global majority standard, ~165 countries)
Left-hand traffic convention (minority standard, ~75 countries including UK, Japan, India)
Vehicle manufacturing industry (designs for dominant market)
Border crossing infrastructure (requires handedness transition zones)
International standards bodies (Vienna Convention on Road Traffic)
key_tensions: Network coordination benefit vs switching cost asymmetry (majority standard gains compounding advantage)
National sovereignty over traffic rules vs cross-border travel efficiency

mechanisms.description: Each additional adopter increases switching cost for remaining holdouts through vehicle design standardization and driver training incompatibility
Road signage, intersection design, highway on-ramps all encode handedness; switching requires rebuilding physical infrastructure
Vehicle production optimizes for majority market; minority-handedness vehicles cost more due to smaller production runs
mechanisms.targets: left-hand traffic countries, consumers in those markets

absences.description: No discussion of whether right-hand vs left-hand traffic has measurable safety differences (relevant if one convention has lower accident rates)
The initial choice mechanism (why some countries chose right vs left) is not addressed, though it may reveal whether the convention was ever contested or simply inherited

axes.structural_delta: The choice between right and left has no inherent functional superiority; value exists only in coordination
axes.primary_observable: Absence of safety or efficiency differential between right-hand and left-hand traffic systems when controlling for infrastructure quality
axes.selection_reason: Foundational mountain establishing that handedness is pure coordination problem; upstream to all other axes

axes.structural_delta: Each additional adopter of the majority standard increases the cost for non-adopters to maintain minority standard
axes.primary_observable: Vehicle manufacturing cost differential between right-hand-drive and left-hand-drive markets; cross-border travel friction at handedness transition points
axes.selection_reason: Distinct observable (network size effects) from mountain; pure coordination mechanism without beneficiary extraction

axes.structural_delta: Sunk infrastructure costs create irreversible path dependence; switching requires rebuilding entire transportation system
axes.primary_observable: Estimated cost to switch handedness (road reconstruction, signage replacement, vehicle fleet turnover); historical examples of countries that switched (Sweden 1967, Samoa 2009)
axes.selection_reason: Distinct from network effects (sunk cost vs coordination benefit); introduces victim structure (countries locked into minority standard)

axes.structural_delta: Majority standard holders exert pressure on minority to switch through trade agreements, vehicle import restrictions, and regional integration requirements
axes.primary_observable: EU accession requirements for traffic standardization; ASEAN harmonization discussions; vehicle import tariff structures favoring majority-handedness vehicles
axes.selection_reason: Introduces beneficiary extraction (majority standard holders gain from forcing minority to bear switching costs); distinct from piton (active coercion vs passive lock-in)

axes.human_readable: Manufacturing Oligopoly Leverage (Industry Standardization as Market Control)
axes.structural_delta: Vehicle manufacturers use majority-standard optimization to extract rents from minority-handedness markets through higher prices and limited model availability
axes.primary_observable: Price differential for right-hand-drive vs left-hand-drive versions of same vehicle model; model availability gaps in minority markets
axes.selection_reason: Distinct beneficiary structure (private industry extraction vs state-level coordination); different observable (price discrimination vs switching costs)

omegas.description: Does right-hand vs left-hand traffic have measurable safety differences? If right-hand driving correlates with lower accident rates due to majority of population being right-eye dominant, the Mountain classification may be incorrect—it would be a Rope of human physiology rather than pure convention.

Was the initial right/left split contested or inherited? If Napoleon's conquests imposed right-hand traffic on continental Europe while Britain retained left-hand as resistance, the convention may encode historical power dynamics rather than arbitrary coordination.

Are switching costs truly prohibitive or merely politically inconvenient? Sweden (1967) and Samoa (2009) successfully switched; if switching is feasible for small/medium countries, the Piton classification may overstate irreversibility.
omegas.source: Dark Matter Probe 3 (Beneficiary Scan) examining who benefits from framing switching as impossible

omegas.description: Do autonomous vehicles eliminate handedness lock-in? If AVs can dynamically adapt to either standard, the entire constraint topology may dissolve within 20 years.
omegas.source: Dark Matter Probe 1 (Operational Medium) examining technological substrate assumptions

fracture_scan.notes: F03 detected: arbitrary_coordination_equilibrium classified as mountain but assumes no safety differential between right-hand and left-hand traffic. If right-eye dominance in majority of population creates measurable safety advantage for right-hand traffic, the convention is not arbitrary—it would be a Rope of human physiology. Generated omega_safety_differential to bound this uncertainty.
